triage.name: Varicose Veins
triage.reason: Common venous disorder with visible and palpable findings on exam; diagnosis largely clinical with clear presentation of leg heaviness, aching and visible veins.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'venous duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']

demographics: More common in women, largely related to pregnancy and hormonal factors
Common in people whose jobs require prolonged standing (retail, nursing, teaching, hairdressing)

risk_factors.text: Prolonged standing or sitting with legs dependent
Prior leg injury or deep vein thrombosis

family_history: Varicose veins in a parent or sibling
Chronic venous insufficiency in the family
social_history: Occupations requiring long periods of standing
Prolonged sitting during travel or desk work

chief_complaints.text: My legs feel heavy and achy by the end of the day
I have twisted, bulging veins on my legs
My ankles swell up in the evening

hpi.onset: Gradual over months to years; often noticed during or after a pregnancy or after years of standing work
hpi.duration: Chronic, present for years and slowly worsening
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; veins become more prominent and symptoms more noticeable over time, worse in warm weather and at the end of the day
hpi.location: Most often the medial calf and thigh, sometimes the posterior calf or lateral leg; usually bilateral but often asymmetric
hpi.radiation: Usually none; discomfort stays in the affected leg
hpi.quality: Dull heaviness, aching, fullness or a tired-leg feeling rather than sharp pain
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually 2–5/10, worse after standing and better with rest
hpi.timing: Worse as the day goes on and after prolonged standing or sitting; best in the morning after lying down overnight
aggravating: Sitting with legs down or crossed
relieving: Elevating the legs above heart level

associated_symptoms.text: Visible twisted, bulging veins under the skin
Aching or throbbing in the legs
Ankle and lower-leg swelling that improves overnight
Itching or burning over the veins
Skin discoloration or darkening near the ankle

pertinent_negatives: Sudden onset of pain and swelling in one leg
Chest pain or shortness of breath
Fever with a red, hot, tender leg
Non-healing ulcer on the foot or toes
Pain that comes on with walking and goes away with rest within a few minutes

positives.text: Leg heaviness and aching worse with standing
Ankle swelling that improves with elevation

negatives: Calf pain and swelling of sudden onset

positives.text: Itching or burning over the veins
Brownish discoloration or dry, scaly skin near the ankle

negatives: Redness, warmth or drainage from the skin
Pain that reliably starts with walking a set distance and stops with rest
Numbness or weakness in the legs

atypical.how_it_differs: Veins enlarge during pregnancy because of increased blood volume and hormonal relaxation of vein walls; symptoms often improve after delivery but may not fully resolve.
More likely to have chronic skin changes, ankle discoloration and even healed or active ulcers, and symptoms may be attributed to arthritis or neuropathy.
missing_classic_features: Symptoms limited to heaviness and aching without skin changes

atypical.how_it_differs: Increased abdominal pressure worsens venous reflux; symptoms are more severe and less responsive to compression alone.
Uncommon; when present it usually reflects a strong family history or an underlying venous malformation, and is often asymptomatic.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable at rest, no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but shifts weight or rubs the legs while standing; mild discomfort
general.severe: Uncomfortable, prefers to sit with the leg elevated, may have visible skin changes
general.critical: Not typical for uncomplicated varicose veins; consider ulceration, bleeding or another cause

findings.maneuver: Inspect both legs from groin to ankle with the patient standing, in good light
findings.finding: Dilated, elongated, tortuous superficial veins that bulge above the skin surface, most often along the medial calf and thigh

findings.maneuver: Palpate the prominent veins with the patient standing
findings.finding: Soft, compressible, non-pulsatile venous cords that empty with elevation

findings.maneuver: Press over the medial malleolus and distal tibia for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the ankle and lower leg, often asymmetric and improving after overnight elevation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the lower legs and ankles
findings.finding: Brownish hyperpigmentation, stasis dermatitis, dry scaly skin, or lipodermatosclerosis near the ankle

findings.maneuver: Inspect the medial and lateral malleolar areas for open wounds
findings.finding: Shallow ulcer with irregular borders and moist granulation tissue near the medial malleolus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin of the thighs and calves
findings.finding: Small red or blue spider veins (telangiectasias) in the same distribution

findings.maneuver: Elevate the leg to empty the veins, place a tourniquet at the saphenofemoral junction, then have the patient stand and release the tourniquet
findings.finding: Rapid refilling of the veins below the tourniquet, localizing incompetent valves

findings.maneuver: Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Palpate the calf and compress the deep veins
findings.finding: No calf tenderness, no palpable cord, no asymmetric swelling of acute onset

findings.maneuver: Inspect and feel the skin of the affected leg
findings.finding: No spreading erythema, warmth, or drainage

findings.maneuver: Palpate the popliteal fossa and groin for a pulsatile mass
findings.finding: No expansile pulsatile mass and no bruit

findings.maneuver: Test sensation and strength in the lower legs

imaging.study: Venous duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities
imaging.preferred_when: Before any intervention and when the diagnosis or anatomy is uncertain

findings.text: Reflux lasting more than 0.5 seconds in the superficial veins (great or small saphenous, or their tributaries) with the patient standing
Dilated, tortuous superficial veins with a measured diameter above the normal range
Competent deep veins with normal phasic flow and no thrombus
Incompetent perforator veins connecting the superficial and deep systems
Reflux or obstruction in the deep veins suggesting post-thrombotic disease

imaging.study: CT venography of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected central venous obstruction or an abdominal or pelvic mass causing secondary varices

findings.text: Compression or obstruction of the iliac or inferior vena cava with enlarged collateral veins
Pelvic or abdominal mass causing extrinsic venous compression

imaging.study: MR venography of the abdomen and pelvis
imaging.preferred_when: When central venous anatomy is needed without ionizing radiation, or when CT contrast is contraindicated

findings.text: Central venous narrowing or occlusion with collateral pathways

imaging.preferred_when: Before compression therapy or intervention when arterial disease is suspected

findings.text: Normal ankle-brachial index (0.9–1.3) confirming adequate arterial supply
Low ankle-brachial index (<0.9) indicating coexisting peripheral arterial disease

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pelvic mass or central venous obstruction as a cause of secondary varices

findings.text: Pelvic mass or enlarged uterus compressing the iliac veins

initial.test: Venous duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities
initial.why: Confirms superficial venous reflux, maps the anatomy, and rules out deep vein thrombosis or obstruction before treatment
Screens for peripheral arterial disease before prescribing compression
initial.only_if: arterial disease is suspected (claudication, absent pulses, diabetes, smoking history)

supporting.why: Defines central venous obstruction or a compressive mass
supporting.only_if: secondary varices or central venous obstruction is suspected (sudden onset, unilateral, abdominal or pelvic symptoms)

supporting.test: MR venography of the abdomen and pelvis
supporting.why: Alternative to CT for central venous anatomy without radiation
supporting.only_if: central venous obstruction is suspected and CT contrast is contraindicated

supporting.why: Looks for a pelvic mass causing venous compression

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical; venous duplex ultrasound is reserved for uncertain diagnosis, atypical findings, or before intervention
Check ankle-brachial index before compression if arterial disease is suspected
Sudden unilateral swelling with calf pain suggests deep vein thrombosis and needs urgent duplex ultrasound
Consider central venous imaging when varices are unilateral, sudden, or associated with abdominal or pelvic symptoms

differential.name: Deep vein thrombosis
differential.why_considered: Leg pain and swelling can be attributed to venous disease, and varicose veins are a risk factor for DVT
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of unilateral calf pain and swelling, especially after immobility, surgery, or a long trip

history: Abrupt onset over hours to days rather than years
Recent immobility, surgery, travel, or prior VTE
Calf pain and tightness rather than chronic heaviness
exam: Unilateral calf tenderness and asymmetric swelling
Warm, tense calf; possible palpable cord
labs: D-dimer elevated (useful mainly to rule out in low-risk patients)
imaging: Non-compressible deep vein with intraluminal thrombus on duplex ultrasound
Absent or reduced phasic flow in the deep veins

differential.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Shares the same underlying venous hypertension and often coexists with varicose veins

history: More prominent swelling, skin changes, and heaviness than visible bulging veins
Symptoms persist despite elevation and compression
exam: Brawny edema, hyperpigmentation, stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis
Healed or active venous ulcer near the medial malleolus
imaging: Deep venous reflux or post-thrombotic obstruction on duplex ultrasound
Superficial reflux may be absent or minimal

differential.name: Peripheral arterial disease
differential.why_considered: Leg discomfort with walking is a common complaint that can be misattributed to venous disease
differential.trigger: Pain that reliably comes on with a set walking distance and resolves with rest, or absent pedal pulses

history: Claudication: cramping pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock provoked by walking and relieved within minutes by rest
Smoking history, diabetes, or known coronary disease
Pain worse with elevation and better with dependency
exam: Diminished or absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Cool, hairless, shiny skin; possible dependent rubor
labs: Diabetes and lipid abnormalities may be present but are not diagnostic
imaging: Arterial stenosis or occlusion on duplex or CT angiography

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: A red, warm, swollen leg can be confused with venous stasis changes
differential.trigger: Fever with a rapidly spreading, red, hot, tender leg

history: Acute onset over hours to days
Often a break in the skin, insect bite, or prior episode
exam: Spreading erythema with a sharp, advancing border
Warmth, tenderness, and possible lymphangitic streaking
imaging: Ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema or abscess but is not required for diagnosis

differential.name: Lymphedema
differential.why_considered: Chronic leg swelling and heaviness overlap with venous disease

history: Gradual, progressive swelling that does not improve overnight
History of lymph node dissection, radiation, or recurrent infection
exam: Non-pitting or brawny edema, often involving the dorsum of the foot (Stemmer sign)
imaging: Duplex ultrasound shows no significant venous reflux

differential.name: Popliteal artery aneurysm
differential.why_considered: A pulsatile mass or fullness behind the knee can be mistaken for varicose veins
differential.trigger: A pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa or a bruit over the knee

history: Often asymptomatic; may present with distal emboli or claudication
History of smoking or other aneurysms
exam: Expansile, pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa
Bruit or thrill over the mass
imaging: Duplex ultrasound shows a fusiform or saccular arterial aneurysm with flow
CT or MR angiography defines the aneurysm and runoff

differential.name: Arteriovenous malformation
differential.why_considered: Enlarged, tortuous vessels in the leg can resemble varicose veins

history: Often present since childhood or adolescence
exam: Warm limb, palpable thrill, or audible bruit
Possible limb length discrepancy or high-output findings
imaging: Duplex ultrasound shows high-velocity arterial flow within the lesion
MRI or angiography demonstrates a nidus and early venous filling

severity.mild: Small, isolated varicose veins with no or minimal symptoms; no skin changes or edema; cosmetic concern only
severity.moderate: Prominent tortuous veins with daily heaviness, aching, and ankle swelling that improves with elevation; no skin breakdown
severity.severe: Extensive varicose veins with persistent edema, skin changes (hyperpigmentation, stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis), or healed ulcer
severity.critical: Not typical for uncomplicated varicose veins; consider active venous ulceration with infection, spontaneous hemorrhage from a varix, or another diagnosis

red_flags.finding: Sudden unilateral calf pain and swelling
red_flags.meaning: Deep vein thrombosis until proven otherwise; needs urgent duplex ultrasound

red_flags.finding: Chest pain, shortness of breath, or hemoptysis
Fever with a red, hot, tender leg
red_flags.meaning: Cellulitis or infected ulcer; needs antibiotics and wound care

red_flags.finding: Active bleeding from a varicose vein
red_flags.meaning: Venous hemorrhage; apply pressure and seek urgent care

red_flags.finding: Non-healing ulcer on the leg or foot
red_flags.meaning: Venous ulcer or arterial insufficiency; requires vascular assessment
Acute arterial ischemia; emergency vascular intervention

complications.name: Superficial thrombophlebitis
clues: Painful, red, warm, tender cord along a superficial vein
Symptoms localized to the varicose vein

complications.name: Venous ulceration
clues: Shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus
History of long-standing swelling and skin changes

complications.name: Bleeding from a varix
clues: Spontaneous or minor-trauma bleeding from a prominent vein
Thin, stretched skin over the vein

complications.name: Deep vein thrombosis
clues: Sudden unilateral calf pain and swelling

special_populations.differences: Veins enlarge due to increased blood volume and hormonal relaxation of vein walls; symptoms often improve after delivery but may not fully resolve. Compression stockings and elevation are first-line; avoid unnecessary procedures.
More likely to have chronic skin changes, ankle discoloration, and healed or active ulcers; symptoms may be attributed to arthritis or neuropathy. Check arterial supply before compression.
Increased abdominal pressure worsens venous reflux; symptoms are more severe and less responsive to compression alone. Weight loss is an important part of management.
Uncommon; when present it usually reflects a strong family history or an underlying venous malformation, and is often asymptomatic. Consider imaging for atypical or unilateral findings.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the veins, and have they changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over months to years with slow progression; sudden onset suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Where are the veins, and is one leg or both legs affected?
key_questions.looking_for: Medial calf and thigh, often bilateral but asymmetric; sudden unilateral findings raise concern for DVT

key_questions.question: How do your legs feel by the end of the day?
key_questions.looking_for: Heaviness, aching, or tiredness that worsens as the day goes on and improves with rest and elevation

key_questions.question: What makes the symptoms better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with prolonged standing, sitting with legs down, warm weather, and menses; better with lying down, elevating the legs, walking, and compression stockings

key_questions.question: Do your ankles or lower legs swell, and does the swelling go away overnight?
key_questions.looking_for: Evening ankle swelling that improves after lying down overnight

key_questions.question: Do you have itching, burning, or cramping in your legs at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching or burning over the veins and night cramps, which support venous disease

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any skin color changes, dryness, or sores near your ankles?
key_questions.looking_for: Brownish discoloration, stasis dermatitis, or an ulcer near the medial malleolus suggesting more advanced disease

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a blood clot in your leg or lung?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior DVT or PE, which increases the risk of post-thrombotic venous disease

key_questions.question: Have you had any leg injuries or leg surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior trauma or surgery that can damage veins and valves

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have varicose veins or vein problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency in a parent or sibling

key_questions.question: What kind of work do you do, and do you stand or sit for long periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupations requiring prolonged standing or sitting with legs dependent

key_questions.question: Have you been pregnant, and did your vein symptoms start or worsen during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, especially multiple pregnancies, as a trigger for vein enlargement

key_questions.question: Are you currently taking any medications, including hormones or birth control?
key_questions.looking_for: Hormonal therapy or oral contraceptives that may influence venous symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you had sudden pain and swelling in one leg, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism requiring urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you had fever with a red, hot, tender leg, or bleeding from a vein?
key_questions.looking_for: Cellulitis, infected ulcer, or venous hemorrhage requiring urgent care

reasoning_points: Gradual onset over months to years of twisted, bulging superficial veins, most often on the medial calf and thigh
Leg heaviness, aching, and fatigue that worsen with prolonged standing and improve with elevation
Evening ankle swelling that improves overnight
Risk factors such as family history, increasing age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, and prolonged standing
Physical exam shows dilated, tortuous, compressible, non-pulsatile superficial veins
Pedal pulses are present and there is no acute calf tenderness, erythema, or warmth
Venous duplex ultrasound, when obtained, shows superficial venous reflux lasting more than 0.5 seconds
Red flags for deep vein thrombosis, cellulitis, or arterial disease are absent

easy: Middle-aged woman with a strong family history and years of standing work
Visible twisted, bulging veins along the medial calf and thigh
Leg heaviness and aching that worsen by the end of the day and improve with elevation
No acute pain, swelling, fever, or skin breakdown
medium: Older adult with ankle swelling and brownish skin discoloration near the ankle
Symptoms attributed to arthritis or neuropathy rather than venous disease
Bilateral but asymmetric findings with coexisting obesity
Need to check arterial supply before recommending compression
hard: Sudden unilateral calf pain and swelling raising concern for deep vein thrombosis
Pulsatile popliteal mass suggesting popliteal artery aneurysm rather than varicose veins
Warm limb with a bruit or thrill suggesting arteriovenous malformation
Non-healing medial malleolar ulcer requiring distinction between venous and arterial causes
Pregnancy with new vein enlargement and swelling requiring conservative management
